case_analysis.focal_point: Whether the Fourth Circuit improperly granted federal habeas relief by departing from AEDPA’s exhaustion and deferential-review requirements and by relying on theories allegedly not presented or exhausted by the prisoner, in a case involving juror exposure to extraneous information and an asserted right to a Remmer hearing.
case_analysis.legal_provision: 28 U.S.C. § 2254 (AEDPA), including exhaustion and deference standards; Sixth Amendment right to an impartial jury/fair trial (as the underlying constitutional right implicated); and the Remmer doctrine governing post-verdict inquiry into external juror influence.
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioners (Maryland officials) argue the Fourth Circuit “flouted” AEDPA by (1) granting relief on a de novo assessment rather than applying AEDPA’s deferential standard to the state-court adjudications, (2) excusing or bypassing exhaustion via an atextual “special circumstances” exception, and (3) effectively deciding the case on a newly constructed Sixth Amendment/structural-error theory that Sweeney did not raise and did not exhaust in state court. They further contend that Supreme Court law does not clearly establish that a juror’s unauthorized visit to a scene triggers Remmer, and that circuit extensions of Remmer cannot substitute for clearly established Supreme Court precedent under AEDPA.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondent (Sweeney) argues summary reversal/certiorari is unwarranted because the Fourth Circuit did not decide the case on arguments invented by the court: the record shows he consistently raised the substance of the issues the Fourth Circuit relied upon, including the need to determine juror taint and the inability to make an informed waiver without that information. He contends the issues “permeated” the proceedings, and any misstep by the Fourth Circuit would be limited to fact-bound application rather than a broad legal departure justifying extraordinary intervention.
key_precedents: Castro v. United States, 540 U.S. 375 (2003) (Scalia, J., concurring)
Major League Baseball Players Ass’n v. Garvey, 532 U.S. 504 (2001)
Eaton v. City of Tulsa, 415 U.S. 697 (1974)
Mayhue v. St. Francis Hosp. of Wichita, Inc., 969 F.2d 919 (10th Cir. 1992)
United States v. Perkins, 748 F.2d 1519 (11th Cir. 1984)
United States v. Hillard, 701 F.2d 1052 (2d Cir. 1983)
United States v. Bassler, 651 F.2d 600 (8th Cir. 1981)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s vehicle point is the strongest counter: if the fair-presentation/exhaustion record is genuinely contested, we should be cautious about using this case to announce broad habeas rules. But even granting her framing that the “core” Sixth Amendment taint-inquiry contention was presented, § 2254(d)(1) still requires clearly established law from this Court, and—as Justice Kagan emphasizes—circuit extensions cannot supply a Remmer-style presumption-and-hearing mandate for a juror’s self-initiated scene visit. On the state-court record, fairminded jurists could agree with Maryland’s disposition, so the Fourth Circuit’s contrary result exceeds AEDPA’s deference and warrants reversal on that narrow ground.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s vehicle/preservation concerns do not overcome AEDPA’s threshold commands: even accepting fair presentation, the Fourth Circuit still had to identify clearly established law from this Court that squarely requires a Remmer-style evidentiary hearing for a juror’s independent scene visit, and it could not obtain relief by extending Remmer beyond its third-party “contact” context. As the Chief Justice and Justice Kagan emphasize, § 2254(d) asks whether the state court’s adjudication was objectively unreasonable, not whether a federal court would have required a more searching inquiry. The Fourth Circuit’s analysis appears to displace the state courts’ primary role by effectively recasting the claim and applying a de novo Sixth Amendment taint framework untethered to clearly established Supreme Court holdings. Because fairminded jurists could agree with the state courts’ resolution on this record, AEDPA bars relief.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s strongest point—that the fair-presentation/exhaustion dispute is fact-bound and makes this a poor vehicle—does not answer AEDPA’s dispositive threshold: even assuming the “core” taint-inquiry contention was presented, § 2254(d)(1) requires clearly established law from this Court that compels the specific Remmer-style presumption-and-hearing procedure on these facts. As the Chief Justice and Justice Kagan emphasize, Remmer’s holding concerns third-party “communication, contact, or tampering,” and circuit extensions cannot supply the missing clearly established rule. Nor is it consistent with AEDPA’s design for a federal court to reframe the case into a broader structural-error/waiver theory and then effectively discount the state court’s prejudice determination without the demanded deference. On this record, fairminded jurists could agree with the state courts’ resolution, so the Fourth Circuit’s grant of relief should be reversed.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: I take the Chief Justice’s and Justice Kagan’s point that § 2254(d)(1) demands a clearly established holding of this Court and that circuit-level extensions of Remmer cannot supply it. But that AEDPA argument presupposes a clean identification of what claim the state courts actually adjudicated and what theory the Fourth Circuit granted relief on; on this disputed, record-bound preservation/fair-presentation posture, I am not prepared to treat Maryland’s framing as dispositive and use this case for summary correction. Even if Remmer does not clearly govern a juror’s self-initiated scene visit, the allegations of extraneous information coupled with the absence of any meaningful taint inquiry present serious due process concerns that counsel against taking this vehicle to announce broad limits on habeas review. As Justice Roberts acknowledges, my vehicle concern “deserves careful attention,” and that concern remains outcome-determinative for me at this threshold stage.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s preservation/vehicle concern is the best argument for respondent, because if the Remmer-style taint-inquiry theory was fairly presented and adjudicated, the case is not easily dismissed on exhaustion grounds. But even taking her premise, § 2254(d)(1) still controls, and as the Chief Justice and Justice Kavanaugh stress, we cannot locate “clearly established Federal law” in circuit extensions of Remmer beyond its third-party contact setting. On this record, the state court’s handling—however imperfect as a matter of best practices—was not shown to be an objectively unreasonable application of this Court’s holdings, and the Fourth Circuit’s reframing risks evading AEDPA’s deference architecture. So I remain for reversal on AEDPA grounds without opining broadly on what procedures might be advisable on direct review.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s preservation/vehicle concern is the most serious objection, but even crediting her best framing that the “core” taint-inquiry complaint was fairly presented, AEDPA still supplies a mandatory threshold: the federal court must test the last reasoned state-court merits decision against this Court’s clearly established holdings, not circuit elaborations. As the Chief Justice and Justice Kagan emphasize, Remmer’s presumption-and-hearing framework arises in the distinct setting of third-party communications or tampering, and extending it to a juror’s self-initiated scene visit is at least debatable among fairminded jurists—foreclosing relief under § 2254(d)(1). Nor may a federal court repackage the claim into a structural-error/waiver theory to evade AEDPA’s channeling, and, even if § 2254(d) were satisfied, Brecht remains an independent, cumulative screen before any writ may issue.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s vehicle/preservation point is the strongest counter: if the Sixth Amendment taint/waiver theory was fairly presented, exhaustion may not supply an easy off-ramp. But even assuming fair presentation, Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan are right that § 2254(d)(1) is the dispositive gatekeeping rule here, and respondent cannot identify clearly established holdings of this Court that require a Remmer-style presumption of prejudice and post-verdict evidentiary hearing for a juror’s self-initiated scene visit (as distinct from third-party “communication, contact, or tampering”). The Fourth Circuit’s reliance on circuit extensions of Remmer and its effective reframing of the claim into a broader structural/waiver theory improperly sidesteps AEDPA deference; fairminded jurists could agree with the state court’s resolution on this record. I therefore remain for reversal on narrow § 2254(d) grounds without opining on best practices for trial courts in managing juror misconduct allegations.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s vehicle point—that fair presentation/exhaustion is contested and fact-bound—deserves attention because we are a court of review, not first view, and we should be cautious about resolving disputed preservation narratives. But even accepting her most generous characterization (as the Chief Justice and Justice Kagan do), AEDPA still requires identification of clearly established Supreme Court law that compels the Remmer-style presumption-and-hearing regime for a juror’s self-initiated scene visit, and our holdings do not clearly extend Remmer beyond third-party contacts. On that premise, fairminded jurists could agree with the state court’s approach on this record, so § 2254(d)(1) bars relief regardless of any close exhaustion questions. I therefore remain with petitioner on the narrow ground that the Fourth Circuit exceeded AEDPA by treating circuit elaborations as clearly established law and effectively reworking the claim to avoid deference.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s vehicle concern is the strongest counterargument: if the Fourth Circuit simply adjudicated the same fairly presented Sixth Amendment taint-inquiry claim, summary reversal might risk deciding a preservation dispute on an incomplete record. But even granting her framing, AEDPA still requires us to measure the last state-court merits adjudication against clearly established holdings of this Court, and—per the Chief Justice and Justice Kagan—Remmer does not clearly establish a mandatory presumption-and-hearing regime for a juror’s self-initiated scene visit, nor can circuit elaborations supply that missing law under § 2254(d)(1). On this record, fairminded jurists could agree with the state court’s disposition, which is enough to foreclose relief under AEDPA’s deference and channeling structure. Accordingly, I remain persuaded that reversal is warranted on § 2254(d) grounds, without opining broadly on best practices for taint inquiries.

John Roberts.reasoning: Because the juror-misconduct claim was adjudicated on the merits in Maryland courts, AEDPA supplies the threshold rule: the Fourth Circuit could grant relief only if the state court’s disposition was not merely wrong but objectively unreasonable under clearly established Supreme Court law on the state-court record. Remmer’s federal supervisory framework does not clearly establish that a state trial court must convene a particular “Remmer hearing” whenever a juror conducts an unauthorized visit; at minimum, fairminded jurists could disagree about whether and how Remmer applies in state collateral review, which forecloses relief under § 2254(d)(1). To the extent the Fourth Circuit relied on an unexhausted or court-constructed structural-error/waiver theory, that approach improperly bypassed AEDPA’s exhaustion and deference structure and undermined comity and finality by effectively re-litigating the case on a different theory than the one the state courts had a full opportunity to address.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: AEDPA makes federal habeas an extraordinary remedy, and the Fourth Circuit improperly displaced the State courts’ primary role by granting relief without adhering to § 2254(d)’s deference and by effectively bypassing exhaustion limits to reach a broader Sixth Amendment/Remmer theory not cleanly presented and adjudicated as such in state court. On the merits, even assuming the claim was exhausted and adjudicated, the State courts’ rejection of relief was not an “unreasonable application” of clearly established Supreme Court law because this Court has not clearly held that a juror’s unauthorized scene visit automatically triggers a Remmer evidentiary hearing or a presumption of prejudice in this context. Granting relief here thus requires extending Remmer beyond its settled facts, something AEDPA forbids on habeas review. Because fairminded jurists could agree with the State courts’ handling of the incident and counsel’s response, § 2254(d) bars relief.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: AEDPA is designed to streamline federal habeas review in service of comity, finality, federalism, and efficiency, and it therefore forbids granting relief unless the state court’s adjudication was contrary to or an unreasonable application of clearly established Supreme Court law. On this record, Remmer clearly establishes a hearing obligation when there is an “unauthorized communication” by an outside third party with a juror, but it does not clearly establish that a juror’s own unauthorized site visit triggers the same presumption and mandatory procedure; circuit extensions of Remmer cannot supply the “clearly established Federal law” § 2254(d) demands. The Fourth Circuit’s approach, as described, effectively substituted its own view of the proper inquiry (and possibly a reframed Sixth Amendment/structural-error conception) for the state court’s Strickland prejudice determination, which is precisely the sort of de novo reweighing AEDPA prohibits. And to the extent the Fourth Circuit relied on an unexhausted or newly constructed theory not presented and tested in the adversarial process, that departure violates the party-presentation principle and improperly expands habeas beyond the claim the prisoner actually litigated.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Applying my issue-preservation and fair-presentation framework, I would not accept Maryland’s premise that the Fourth Circuit granted relief on wholly unpresented theories: on this record, Sweeney repeatedly pressed the core contention that juror exposure to extraneous information required a meaningful taint inquiry and that any waiver could not be knowing without that information, which fairly presented the operative Sixth Amendment problem to the federal courts. Because the asserted AEDPA/exhaustion objection turns on what arguments and theories were actually preserved and presented below—and Maryland’s characterization is contested and fact-bound—I would not treat this as a proper vehicle for extraordinary correction, and I would decline to disturb the Fourth Circuit’s disposition at this stage. Separately, the underlying allegations (an unauthorized juror scene visit and the absence of an adequate post-verdict inquiry) raise serious due process concerns about the reliability of the state procedure, reinforcing caution before using certiorari or summary reversal to foreclose merits review on a disputed preservation record. The appropriate course is to address AEDPA-deference limits in a case where the deference/preservation question is clearly and cleanly teed up.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: AEDPA requires a federal habeas court to ask first whether the state court’s adjudication was contrary to, or an unreasonable application of, this Court’s clearly established law—not to decide de novo whether a better procedure (like a Remmer-style hearing) should have been used. On these facts (a juror’s unauthorized scene visit and resulting questions about extraneous information), no holding of this Court clearly establishes that Remmer’s presumption/hearing requirement applies absent a third-party “communication, contact, or tampering,” so the Fourth Circuit could not rely on circuit extensions to supply the missing rule under § 2254(d)(1). And to the extent the court of appeals granted relief on a theory not fairly presented and exhausted in state court (an unwaivable/structural Sixth Amendment theory tied to the lack of a taint hearing), that approach conflicts with AEDPA’s exhaustion framework rather than operating as any permissible “special circumstances” bypass. The proper disposition is therefore to reverse, because the state court’s handling of the juror-misconduct issue was not shown to be unreasonably contrary to clearly established Supreme Court precedent as AEDPA demands.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: AEDPA supplies a mandatory threshold: a federal court “shall not” grant relief unless it applies § 2254(d) to the last state-court adjudication on the merits, and here the Fourth Circuit’s approach appears to have bypassed that constraint by treating the juror-taint/Remmer issue in substantial part as a de novo federal question and by invoking a “special circumstances” route around ordinary exhaustion limits. Even if one assumes the underlying Sixth Amendment concern is serious, federal habeas relief cannot rest on an unexhausted or newly reframed theory; AEDPA’s focus is the reasonableness of what the state courts actually decided, not what a federal court might decide in the first instance. Nor may circuit-law extensions of Remmer substitute for “clearly established Federal law, as determined by the Supreme Court,” and—separately—any relief would still have to clear Brecht’s harmless-error inquiry in addition to AEDPA’s demanding deference screen. Because the Fourth Circuit’s grant of relief appears inconsistent with AEDPA’s exhaustion and § 2254(d) limits keyed to the state courts’ merits resolution, I would vote to reverse.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The issue in this case is narrow: under AEDPA, the federal court may grant relief only if the state court’s decision was contrary to, or an unreasonable application of, clearly established Supreme Court law, and the federal court must enforce exhaustion and other gatekeeping rules before reaching constitutional merits. Here, the Fourth Circuit effectively treated Remmer as clearly establishing a required post-verdict hearing for juror exposure to extraneous information in these circumstances (including an unauthorized juror scene visit), but this Court has not clearly extended Remmer beyond third-party “communication, contact, or tampering,” and circuit extensions cannot supply “clearly established” law under § 2254(d)(1). In addition, AEDPA’s procedural limits cannot be bypassed via an atextual “special circumstances” exception or by resolving the case on a new Sixth Amendment/structural-error theory not properly presented and exhausted in state court; federal habeas review is record-bound and deferential to the state adjudication. Applying those gatekeeping principles and § 2254(d)(1) as written, the Fourth Circuit’s grant of habeas relief should be reversed.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: AEDPA requires a federal habeas court to apply deferential review to the state court’s adjudication and to respect exhaustion as a threshold constraint, not to create a “special circumstances” workaround from statutory silence simply because relief would otherwise be hard to obtain. On this record, the Fourth Circuit’s grant of relief appears to depend on extending Remmer beyond what this Court has clearly held—particularly as to whether a juror’s unauthorized scene visit necessarily triggers a Remmer-type evidentiary hearing—and AEDPA forbids using circuit precedent to "refine" Supreme Court generalities into a specific rule. Relatedly, to the extent the Fourth Circuit relied on a Sixth Amendment/structural-error or waiver theory not fairly presented and exhausted in state court (or not addressed below), that approach conflicts with party-presentation and “court of review, not first view” norms. Because no clearly established Supreme Court decision squarely requires a Remmer hearing on these facts, and because exhaustion/deference constraints cannot be bypassed by judicial invention, I would vote to reverse.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: AEDPA’s text makes exhaustion and deference the gateway: a federal court “shall not” grant relief unless the claim was first fairly presented to the State, and it may not upset a state merits adjudication unless § 2254(d)’s demanding standards are met. On this record, the Fourth Circuit appears to have granted relief on a Sixth Amendment/structural-error theory about juror taint and the absence of a Remmer hearing that (as the dissent notes) was not actually pressed through the state courts (or even the federal district court), which means exhaustion was not satisfied and de novo review was not available. Even if a related juror-misconduct claim was litigated, AEDPA limits relief to violations of “clearly established” Supreme Court law, and extending Remmer’s federal-prosecution framework to these facts cannot substitute for that constraint. The court of appeals’ reliance on an atextual “special circumstances” carve-out and its failure to anchor relief in § 2254(d)’s posture and limits departs from AEDPA’s channeling design and warrants reversal.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether the Fourth Circuit improperly granted federal habeas relief by departing from AEDPA’s limits—raising or relying on unexhausted/unpresented Sixth Amendment theories and failing to apply AEDPA deference—rather than confining review to Sweeney’s exhausted ineffective-assistance claim.
case_analysis.legal_provision: 28 U.S.C. § 2254 (AEDPA) (including exhaustion and deferential review requirements) and the Sixth Amendment right to an impartial jury/fair trial (as implicated by alleged juror exposure to extraneous information and Remmer-type procedures).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioners (Maryland officials) argue the Fourth Circuit ‘flouted’ AEDPA by (1) effectively inventing and deciding new Sixth Amendment/structural-error theories that Sweeney did not properly raise or exhaust in state court or federal habeas, (2) invoking an atextual ‘special circumstances’ exception (purportedly from Frisbie and Granberry) to bypass exhaustion, and (3) refusing to apply AEDPA’s deferential standard even to the one exhausted Strickland ineffective-assistance claim; they contend this warrants Supreme Court intervention (potentially summary reversal) because the panel’s approach is untenable under binding precedent and violates party-presentation principles.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondent (Sweeney) argues summary reversal is inappropriate because the Fourth Circuit applied Supreme Court precedent to an unusual factual record; the court did not decide the case on arguments never presented because Sweeney’s filings raised the core points the Fourth Circuit relied upon and the issues permeated the proceedings; to the extent the court made any mistake, it was factbound and not a vehicle for broad legal correction, and Maryland overstates any party-presentation or exhaustion problem.
key_precedents: Major League Baseball Players Ass’n v. Garvey, 532 U.S. 504 (2001)
Eaton v. City of Tulsa, 415 U.S. 697 (1974)
Mayhue v. St. Francis Hosp. of Wichita, Inc., 969 F.2d 919 (10th Cir. 1992)
United States v. Perkins, 748 F.2d 1519 (11th Cir. 1984)
United States v. Hillard, 701 F.2d 1052 (2d Cir. 1983)
United States v. Bassler, 651 F.2d 600 (8th Cir. 1981)

John Roberts.reasoning: The strongest respondent-side argument is that the juror-contact allegations are so serious that a federal court should reach the merits notwithstanding imperfect exhaustion, but AEDPA does not permit that equitable end-run. As Justice Kagan underscored, the Fourth Circuit effectively pivoted from the exhausted Strickland claim to broader Remmer/impartial-jury theories Maryland courts never adjudicated in that posture, and then failed to apply the required “fairminded jurist” constraint to the one claim that was adjudicated on the merits. Justice Alito is also right that whatever discretion Granberry suggests cannot override Congress’s command that relief “shall not be granted” unless § 2254(b)–(d) is satisfied, on the state-court record and claim-by-claim. The proper disposition is reversal (or vacatur and remand) requiring analysis confined to the exhausted ineffective-assistance claim under § 2254(d).

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The respondent’s strongest argument is that the juror-contact allegations are so grave that a federal court may treat them as a freestanding Sixth Amendment/Remmer problem notwithstanding imperfect state presentation. But AEDPA forecloses that move: as Justice Alito and the Chief emphasize, § 2254(b)–(c) requires claim-by-claim fair presentment, and § 2254(d) makes the state-court merits adjudication the mandatory focal point before relief “shall” be granted. The Fourth Circuit’s “special circumstances” bypass and reframing of an exhausted Strickland claim into an unexhausted structural/impartial-jury theory amounts to an end-run around Congress’s carefully crafted limits and cannot be squared with our cases warning against extending precedent beyond its holdings. Even taking the facts seriously, federal habeas is not roving error correction; the proper disposition is reversal (or at least vacatur and remand) requiring analysis confined to the exhausted claim under § 2254(d).

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The respondent’s strongest contention is that the juror-contact allegations are so serious that a federal court may reach the merits notwithstanding imperfect exhaustion, invoking Granberry-style discretion or a Remmer-like structural framework. But as Justice Kagan and the Chief Justice explain, AEDPA is claim-specific and makes exhaustion and § 2254(d) deference mandatory constraints; a court of appeals cannot recast an exhausted Strickland claim into a distinct, effectively unexhausted Sixth Amendment/Remmer theory and then award relief on something approaching de novo review. Even assuming troubling facts, Congress foreclosed an atextual “special circumstances” bypass of the statutory sequencing, and the Fourth Circuit’s departure from party presentation only underscores the error. The proper course is reversal (or at least vacatur and remand) requiring analysis confined to the exhausted ineffective-assistance claim under § 2254(d).

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The respondent’s strongest point is that juror-contact allegations go to the heart of the Sixth Amendment and may warrant prompt federal attention when state processes appear to fail. But as Justice Kagan and the Chief emphasize, AEDPA’s architecture is claim-by-claim: federal courts cannot recast an exhausted Strickland claim into a distinct Remmer/impartial-jury theory never fairly presented to Maryland courts and then grant relief without identifying the last state-court merits adjudication and applying § 2254(d)’s fairminded-jurist constraint. However troubling the facts, bypassing exhaustion and deference here would effectively deprive the State of a meaningful opportunity to adjudicate the specific federal theory and would invite precisely the kind of categorical, non-statutory “special circumstances” exception AEDPA forecloses. The proper course is reversal, or at minimum vacatur and remand for analysis confined to the exhausted ineffective-assistance claim under § 2254(d).

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The strongest respondent argument is that the juror-contact allegations are so grave that a federal court should reach the issue even if the theory was imperfectly presented in state court. But as the Chief Justice underscores, AEDPA makes the state court’s merits adjudication of the claim actually presented the “main event,” and §2254(d) bars relief unless that decision is unreasonable on the state-court record; the Fourth Circuit instead appears to have recast an exhausted Strickland claim into broader Remmer/impartial-jury theories and then proceeded on something like de novo review. Whatever limited discretion Granberry/Wood might allow regarding exhaustion, it cannot supply an atextual “special circumstances” route to decide a distinct, unexhausted constitutional claim and grant relief without satisfying §2254(b)–(d)’s claim-by-claim constraints. On that understanding, reversal (or at least vacatur and remand for proper §2254(d) analysis of the exhausted Strickland claim) is the only course consistent with AEDPA’s text and our precedents, as Justice Gorsuch and Justice Alito also emphasize.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The strongest respondent argument is that the juror-contact allegations are so grave that a federal court should reach them notwithstanding imperfect exhaustion, perhaps by treating the problem as structural under Remmer or invoking Granberry-style discretion. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan explain, AEDPA’s sequencing leaves no room for an atextual “special circumstances” bypass: where the state court adjudicated the claim presented, § 2254(d) supplies an independent, mandatory limitation, and where the federal court pivots to a new Sixth Amendment/Remmer theory not fairly presented, § 2254(b) bars merits relief on that distinct claim. The Fourth Circuit’s reframing of an exhausted Strickland claim into freestanding impartial-jury/hearing-right theories, coupled with its failure to anchor relief in the last state-court merits adjudication under the fairminded-jurist standard, is legal error under the statute’s “shall not be granted” command. The appropriate course is reversal or, at minimum, vacatur and remand for an analysis confined to the exhausted Strickland claim under § 2254(d).

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The strongest respondent-side point is that serious juror-contact allegations implicate core Sixth Amendment fairness and therefore warrant federal intervention even if the precise theory was not cleanly exhausted. But as the Chief Justice and Justice Kagan explained, AEDPA is claim-by-claim: §2254(b) requires fair presentment of the specific federal claim to the state courts, and §2254(d) independently bars relief unless the state court’s merits adjudication of the claim actually presented was unreasonable on the state-court record. The Fourth Circuit’s move—recasting an exhausted Strickland claim into distinct Remmer/impartial-jury theories and then effectively proceeding without the “fairminded jurist” constraint—amounts to an atextual bypass that Congress did not authorize. Troubling facts cannot supply a free-floating equitable exception to AEDPA’s mandatory sequencing and limits, so reversal (or at least vacatur and remand for proper §2254(d) review of the exhausted claim) is required.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The strongest respondent argument is that the Remmer-style juror-exposure theory is merely additional evidentiary support for the exhausted Strickland claim, so the federal court could reach it without treating it as a new claim. But as the Chief Justice and Justice Kagan underscore, AEDPA operates claim-by-claim: a court cannot transform an ineffective-assistance vehicle into a freestanding Sixth Amendment impartial-jury/hearing-right theory—different elements and remedial posture—without fair presentment and without identifying and deferring to the last state-court merits adjudication under § 2254(d). The Fourth Circuit’s atextual “special circumstances” bypass of exhaustion, combined with its failure to apply § 2254(d)’s fairminded-jurist constraint to the exhausted claim, exceeds the boundary Congress set for federal habeas review. Reversal (or vacatur and remand limited to the exhausted Strickland claim under § 2254(d) on the state-court record) is therefore warranted.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The respondent’s best point is that the juror-contact allegations are so serious that a federal court should reach them notwithstanding imperfect state-court presentation, perhaps invoking Granberry-style discretion. But AEDPA’s text and procedural architecture are claim-specific: § 2254(b)–(c) requires fair presentment of the federal theory to the state courts, and § 2254(d) makes the state court’s merits adjudication of the claim actually presented the mandatory focal point before relief may issue. As Justice Kagan and the Chief emphasize, the Fourth Circuit effectively recast an exhausted Strickland claim into distinct Remmer/impartial-jury theories and then proceeded on something like de novo review—an end run around the gatekeeping Congress enacted. However troubling the facts, the proper course is to confine review to the exhausted ineffective-assistance claim and apply § 2254(d)’s deference (or require exhaustion of any distinct Sixth Amendment theory), which supports reversal or vacatur and remand.

John Roberts.reasoning: AEDPA makes the state-court merits adjudication the “main event,” and federal habeas relief may issue only if the state court’s resolution of the claim actually presented was not merely wrong but unreasonable under § 2254(d) on the state-court record. On this record, the Fourth Circuit’s grant of relief appears to rest on Sixth Amendment juror-bias/Remmer-type theories and procedural suppositions that were not fairly presented and exhausted in state court (and thus not properly before the federal court), and it then failed to apply § 2254(d)’s deferential lens to the one claim that was exhausted—ineffective assistance under Strickland. There is no freestanding “special circumstances” license to bypass exhaustion or to recast a Strickland claim into a different, structural Sixth Amendment claim and decide it de novo; doing so conflicts with AEDPA’s statutory limits and with party-presentation principles. Because the court of appeals effectively treated habeas as ordinary error correction rather than collateral review constrained by § 2254(d), the judgment should be reversed.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: AEDPA makes exhaustion and strict claim presentation a threshold requirement, and on this record the Fourth Circuit appears to have granted relief by relying on Sixth Amendment/Remmer-type structural-error theories that were not fairly presented to (and adjudicated by) the state courts as the specific federal basis for relief, effectively treating Congress’s “carefully crafted limits” as a nullity. Even if Sweeney preserved an ineffective-assistance claim, the court still had to apply § 2254(d)’s deferential “fairminded jurist” constraint to the state court’s Strickland adjudication rather than substituting de novo judgment about what procedures should have occurred. To the extent the Fourth Circuit’s result depended on extending this Court’s jury-impartiality precedents beyond their holdings or converting noncontrolling language into a broader constitutional rule, AEDPA forbids relief absent clearly established law requiring that outcome. Federal habeas is not ordinary error correction; it is reserved for “extreme malfunctions,” and the panel’s approach improperly dilutes AEDPA’s thresholds and deference.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: AEDPA establishes a habeas-specific, statute-driven regime designed to promote comity, finality, and federalism, and it does not permit a court of appeals to grant relief by pivoting to Sixth Amendment juror-bias/Remmer-style theories that the prisoner did not fairly present and exhaust in state court. Whatever discretion Granberry once recognized to overlook a forfeited nonexhaustion defense in unusual pre-AEDPA circumstances cannot justify affirmatively bypassing § 2254(b)–(c)’s exhaustion commands—much less using an atextual “special circumstances” exception to reach and decide issues not litigated by the parties. On the one claim that was properly before the federal courts (ineffective assistance), the Fourth Circuit was still bound to apply § 2254(d)’s deferential standard rather than reassessing the trial record as if on de novo review; granting relief without identifying a clearly established holding of this Court that the state court unreasonably applied is precisely what AEDPA forbids. The panel’s departure from party presentation and AEDPA’s strict limits warrants reversal.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: AEDPA’s threshold limits require federal courts to confine merits review to claims the state courts had a full and fair opportunity to adjudicate, and here the Fourth Circuit acknowledged that Sweeney had not presented to the Maryland courts (and thus not exhausted) the standalone Sixth Amendment impartial-jury/Remmer-type theories it ultimately used to justify relief. Granberry and Wood permit limited appellate discretion to address a State’s forfeited defenses, but they do not authorize a federal court to bypass exhaustion and then grant relief on new, unadjudicated constitutional theories—especially where doing so prevents the state courts from ever issuing a merits ruling that would define (and “trigger”) the proper AEDPA deference framework. On the one claim Sweeney did exhaust—trial-ineffective-assistance—the federal court was required to apply § 2254(d)’s deferential review to the state court’s Strickland adjudication rather than effectively converting the case into a de novo structural-error inquiry. Because the panel’s approach short-circuited AEDPA’s claim-by-claim posture and displaced Strickland’s case-specific analysis with unexhausted theories, I would vote to reverse.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: AEDPA requires a federal habeas court to confine itself to the claim the prisoner actually presented and exhausted in state court, and then to ask only whether the state court’s rejection of that claim was “so lacking in justification” as to be beyond fairminded disagreement. Here, the Fourth Circuit’s decision appears to grant relief by pivoting from Sweeney’s properly exhausted Strickland ineffective-assistance theory to broader Sixth Amendment juror-impartiality/Remmer-style theories (and a “special circumstances” exhaustion bypass) that were not litigated as such in state court or framed as the operative federal claim—an approach that both disregards AEDPA’s exhaustion/party-presentation limits and fails to apply §2254(d)’s required deference to the one exhausted claim. Even if the underlying juror-contact facts are troubling, AEDPA’s framework controls what “legal and factual materials” and what theories can justify relief, and a federal court cannot use novel reframing to evade those constraints. On this record, the proper course is reversal or at least a remand to apply §2254(d) to the exhausted Strickland claim and to respect exhaustion as to any distinct Remmer-type claim.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: AEDPA requires a federal habeas court to identify the last state-court adjudication on the merits of the federal claim actually presented and then ask whether that decision survives § 2254(d)’s demanding limits; it is legal error to bypass that inquiry and grant relief on a de novo or newly framed constitutional theory. On this record, the Fourth Circuit appears to have pivoted away from Sweeney’s exhausted Strickland ineffective-assistance claim and instead relied on broader, effectively unexhausted Sixth Amendment/Remmer-style theories (and an atextual “special circumstances” excuse for nonexhaustion) that the state courts did not adjudicate on the merits in the form the panel embraced. Because § 2254(d) is an independent, mandatory bar—habeas relief “shall not be granted” unless its terms are satisfied—the panel could not grant relief without first applying AEDPA deference to the relevant state-court merits decision (and, where applicable, requiring the petitioner to clear every independent hurdle rather than substituting a different standard). The proper course is to reverse (or at least vacate and remand) for an analysis confined to the exhausted claim and the constraints AEDPA imposes.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The issue in this case is narrow: whether the Fourth Circuit, in granting § 2254 relief, stayed within AEDPA’s exhaustion and deference limits or instead recast the case into new, unexhausted Sixth Amendment/Remmer-style theories. On this record, the panel majority appeared to bypass exhaustion by invoking an atextual “special circumstances” rationale and then decided unpresented constitutional claims (trial-judge duty to investigate, confrontation/impartial-jury violations, and a freestanding hearing requirement), contrary to party-presentation principles and AEDPA’s claim-by-claim structure. Even as to the one exhausted Strickland ineffective-assistance claim, AEDPA required deference to the state court’s adjudication of that specific claim and forbade granting relief absent clearly established Supreme Court law; the panel’s approach resembles the kind of reframing and nondeferential merits review this Court has repeatedly rejected. The proper course is to reverse and require any federal review to be confined to exhausted claims and conducted under § 2254(d)’s stringent standard.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: AEDPA supplies the controlling procedural framework here: federal habeas relief must be confined to claims fairly presented and exhausted in state court and then reviewed with § 2254(d) deference to the state court’s adjudication. On this record, the Fourth Circuit appears to have moved beyond Sweeney’s exhausted Strickland ineffective-assistance theory and effectively granted relief on broader, Remmer-style Sixth Amendment/juror-exposure theories that were not properly presented and exhausted, while also failing to apply AEDPA’s deferential lens to the one claim that was. That departure contravenes both AEDPA’s channeling limits and party-presentation principles by allowing a court to supply and decide a different constitutional theory than the parties litigated through the state system. The proper course is to enforce the boundary AEDPA draws—review only the exhausted claim under § 2254(d)—which means the Fourth Circuit’s grant of relief cannot stand on the rationale it used.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: AEDPA’s text and structure require a federal habeas court to confine merits relief to claims the prisoner properly exhausted in state court and, for any claim adjudicated on the merits there, to apply § 2254(d)’s deferential standard rather than conduct de novo review or aggregate perceived trial errors into a free-floating Sixth Amendment violation. On this record, the Fourth Circuit’s decision to reach (and effectively grant relief on) Remmer-type juror-exposure/impartial-jury theories that were not fairly presented through the state system—and to invoke an atextual “special circumstances” bypass drawn from pre-AEDPA cases like Frisbie and Granberry—impermissibly circumvents the gatekeeping Congress codified and later tightened. And even as to the one exhausted vehicle (ineffective assistance under Strickland), AEDPA demands deference to the state court’s resolution unless it was contrary to or an unreasonable application of clearly established Supreme Court law, which the panel’s de novo, record-reweighing approach fails to respect. Maintaining the remedial boundary lines Congress drew in § 2254 means the Fourth Circuit’s grant of relief cannot stand on unexhausted theories or on a nondeferential mode of review.
